1 
Centre of Pressure Filtering for a Wii Balance 
Board Balloon Game  
SSRP Project 3   Experimental report  
Four causal filters were evaluated in a body controlled balloon task and by replaying the same recorded inputs 
through every filter. The experiment demonstrates a working acquisition and game pipeline, while separating 
measured behaviour from theoretical predictions and limitations of the study design. 
Team member Student ID Assigned experimental filter 
Dharti Prakash Parmar 25110228 Alpha beta 
Arham Gandhi 25110045 Butterworth low pass 
Alka Kushwaha 25110025 Moving average 
Akshat Shah 25110019 Median spike 
 
Abstract 
A Nintendo Wii Balance Board supplied four corner loads to a desktop Unity balloon game. A Python file to UDP 
bridge transmitted calibrated loads, while Unity calculated centre of pressure (CoP), applied one causal filter 
and mapped the result to the absolute position of a blue pointer. Four participants each played four nominal 90 
second rounds with one assigned filter, producing 16 round datasets and six scheduled minutes per participant. 
No VR headset was used. 
Independent calculations confirmed approximately 20 Hz acquisition. The three sample median and five sample 
moving average had approximately 47 and 98 ms interpolated signal lag. The Butterworth coefficients were 
designed for 2.5 Hz at 50 Hz but ran at about 20 Hz, producing an effective 1 Hz cutoff and approximately 233 
ms lag. The alpha beta filter had approximately 7 ms interpolated lag; this is a sub-sample estimate, not 
measured device latency. Common-input replay demonstrated the smoothing versus delay trade-off. Gameplay 
scores cannot identify the best filter because each participant used a different filter and seeded spawn 
sequences diverged during play. 
Recordings were collected on 5 November 2026 according to the supplied file names. Calculations and technical verification we re 
revised on 10 November 2026. The original recordings were not modified.

2 
Objective 
The project investigated how causal discrete time filters change CoP movement before it is used for interactive 
game control. The objectives were to acquire and preserve board measurements, calculate horizontal and 
vertical CoP, compare smoothing and delay, and relate the filtered signals to observed task outcomes without 
treating participant differences as filter effects. 
Experimental Design 
System overview 
 
Figure 1. Physical acquisition, local UDP transport, Unity processing and preserved data. Walker supported board connection; the 
Recorder supplied the text rows consumed by the bridge. 
Software and responsibilities 
Component Role in the experiment 
WiiBalanceWalker v0.5 Supported Bluetooth connection to the board 
Wii Balance Board Recorder v1.0.0 Board calibration and continuously appended measurement file 
Python 3 bridge Read complete rows, assign sequence numbers, preserve an audit and send JSON UDP packets 
Unity 6000.6.6f1 and C# CoP, validity checks, selected filter, calibration mapping, game and trial logs  
Independent report analysis Python 3.12.14 and NumPy 2.3.5; explicit causal recurrences and FFT calculations  
 
The live endpoint was UDP 127.0.0.1 port 5005 on the same computer. The bridge used Python standard-library 
modules and did not perform the experimental filtering. The four assessed filters ran inside Unity, once per 
new accepted sample, not once per rendered frame. vJoy was not the live data transport for these UDP trials. 
Software source: COP-MAIN-PROJECT, branch main [1]. The precise Python version used during acquisition was not recorded, so 
the version above refers only to the independent report analysis.

3 
Signal acquisition and calibration 
What one sample contained 
The Recorder text row contained time, Recorder CoP x and y, four calibrated corner loads, total weight and four 
raw sensor counts. The bridge transmitted the four calibrated loads with a sequence number and source 
timestamp. Unity recomputed CoP rather than using the Recorder CoP columns. The Recorder corner loads 
were labelled in newtons; the game used their ratios, which are dimensionless. 
W = FL + FR + RL + RR 
CoPₓ = (FR + RR) − (FL + RL)W      CoPᵧ = (FL + FR) − (RL + RR)W  
FL, FR, RL and RR denote front left, front right, rear left and rear right. The configured convention made right 
lean positive x and forward lean positive y. Horizontal CoP was mediolateral (ML); vertical game control used 
anterior posterior (AP) CoP. These are balance ratios, not centimetres. Unity rejected non-finite or negative 
corner loads and total load below 10. 
Board calibration and participant calibration 
The team reported zero-load calibration followed by a known 4 kg mass placed centrally in the Recorder. This 
corrected the board measurement scale and offsets. It was separate from the five-point participant calibration 
in Unity: centre, comfortable left, right, forward and backward lean. 
The implemented Unity capture used the latest valid raw CoP sample at each button press, not a timed 
average. Directional ranges had to exceed 0.02 CoP units from centre. The filtered signal was centred and 
divided by the applicable positive or negative range. A per-axis dead zone then removed small movements and 
continuously remapped the remaining range before clamping to −1 to +1. 
q = filtered CoP − centrecomfortable directional range 
u = 0 if |q| ≤ d; otherwise u = sign(q) min(1,(|q| − d)/(1 − d)) 
The source default dead zone was 0.08 on each axis. Participant-specific calibration values and a build identifier 
were not present in the supplied CSV headers; their exact values cannot be reconstructed from these files. A 
larger calibrated range reduces the pointer displacement produced by the same lean, so simply asking for a 
wider lean is not a general calibration fix. 
For future trials, average several seconds of quiet stance and repeat comfortable directional holds. This is a recommendation , 
not a description of the single-sample captures used in the recorded experiment.

4 
Experimental protocol and game 
Participants and rounds 
Four team members participated. Akshat used the median filter, Alka the moving average, Arham the 
Butterworth filter and Dharti the alpha beta filter. Each participant played four nominal 90 second rounds with 
the assigned filter throughout. Four rounds provided six scheduled minutes, meeting the five minute minimum. 
There was no measured unfiltered gameplay baseline and no participant crossed over between filters. 
The intended order of seeds was 104729, 130363, 155921 and 196613. The logs record FixedSeeded mode. 
Each round spawned 44 balloons, not 40. Balloons still active at round completion were neither hits nor misses 
and were excluded from the resolved-target hit rate. 
Game interaction 
Leaning moved the blue pointer, not the camera. The calibrated x and y values set absolute pointer position 
within approximately ±1.6 horizontal and ±1.0 vertical Unity units around a fixed interaction plane. Holding a 
lean held a position; it did not continuously integrate pointer velocity. A hit occurred when the pointer and 
balloon trigger colliders touched. A miss occurred when a balloon passed z = 2.75 without being hit. 
Property Configured value 
Spawn coordinates x −1.55 to 1.55; y 0.75 to 2.55; z 7 to 12 
Base approach speed 0.70 to 1.15 Unity units per second 
Nominal phases 0 to 30 s; 30 to 60 s; 60 to 90 s 
Spawn intervals by phase 2.4 s; 2.1 s; 1.8 s 
Speed multipliers by phase 0.85; 1.00; 1.10 
Display Desktop monitor; pointer, balloons, score, misses, timer and countdown 
 
What fixed seeds did and did not guarantee 
Seeded random numbers made the initial spawns repeatable, but spawn candidate rejection also depended on 
currently active balloons. Player hits changed those active balloons and therefore later random-number 
consumption. Comparing logged spawn coordinates and speeds across participants found only 17, 14, 6 and 5 
identical initial spawns respectively for the four seeds. The trials were seeded but were not fully identical target 
presentations. 
Future comparisons should precompute complete target lists independent of gameplay. This report therefore avoids describing 
the recorded rounds as fully matched sequences.

5 
Causal filter implementations 
Each selected filter processed x and y separately using the same parameters. Causal means that an output used 
only the present and previous samples. No forward-backward or zero-phase filtering was used for live control 
or for the comparisons reported here. 
Table 1. Assessed filter parameters and memory 
Filter Parameters Structure 
Median spike N = 3 samples Nonlinear trailing window 
Moving average N = 5 samples FIR with five equal coefficients 
Butterworth low pass Order 2; design 2.5 Hz at 50 Hz Recursive IIR; realised cutoff about 1 Hz at 20 Hz 
Alpha beta α = 0.85; β = 0.05 Position and velocity prediction with correction 
 
Moving average and median 
y[n] = x[n] + x[n−1] + ⋯ + x[n−N+1]N  
y[n] = median(x[n],x[n−1],x[n−2]) for N = 3 
The finite impulse response (FIR) moving average combines five inputs spanning four intervals, or 200 ms at 20 
Hz. Its group delay is two samples, or 100 ms. The median selects the middle of three ordered values; it 
removes an isolated one-sample spike in a constant baseline but can alter brief genuine movements. For a 
monotonic sequence after startup, it returns the previous sample. Both implementations use the available 
samples during startup. 
Second order Butterworth 
y[n] = b₀x[n] + b₁x[n−1] + b₂x[n−2] − a₁y[n−1] − a₂y[n−2] 
The verified coefficients were b = [0.02008337, 0.04016673, 0.02008337] and a = [1, −1.56101808, 
0.64135154]. The highest output delay is two samples, making this a second-order difference equation. This 
infinite impulse response (IIR) filter reuses earlier outputs, giving it a decaying memory beyond two samples. 
Alpha beta predictor 
p⁻[n] = p[n−1] + v[n−1]Δt;     e[n] = x[n] − p⁻[n] 
p[n] = p⁻[n] + αe[n];     v[n] = v[n−1] + (β/Δt)e[n] 
The output is p[n]. Initially, position equals the first input and velocity is zero. Unity clamps Δt to 0.001 to 0.25 
s. With fixed Δt and gains the position response is linear time-invariant (LTI) after initialization. Its transfer 
function follows; irregular changes in Δt do not generally preserve this response. 
H(z) = 0.85 − 0.80z⁻¹1 − 1.10z⁻¹ + 0.15z⁻²

6 
Timing audit and implementation verification 
Measured rate rather than requested rate 
Acquisition rate was calculated from the original Recorder time column and independently from Unity receive 
timestamps. Complete Recorder files gave 19.986 to 19.996 Hz, including intervals outside gameplay. The 16 
game logs gave 19.978 to 20.003 Hz. The mean was therefore approximately 20 Hz, corresponding to a 50 ms 
average sample period, not 50 Hz. 
f̂ₛ = M − 1t[M−1] − t[0]     T̄ₛ = 1/f̂ₛ 
The median interval was about 47 ms, which differed from the 50 ms mean because intervals were not 
perfectly uniform. Across complete Recorder files, the 5th to 95th percentile range was approximately 44 to 63 
ms. Frequency-domain calculations used a nominal 20 Hz sample-index model without resampling. Their 
frequencies and delays are approximate physical-time interpretations of this mildly irregular stream. 
Two separate timing problems 
First, the bridge default interpreted the Recorder Time column as milliseconds although the recorded values 
were seconds. It divided source times by 1000. For example, a Recorder time of 0.049 s became 0.000049 in the 
audit. Unity source time consequently spanned about 0.09 instead of 90 s per round. Unity then floored most 
processing intervals at 0.0001 s; the alpha beta filter separately clamped them to 0.001 s. Receive timestamps 
and original Recorder timestamps were retained for this audit. 
Second, Butterworth coefficients were designed using a nominal 50 Hz rate. The coefficients themselves did not 
use the timestamp interval on each call. Applying them at 20 Hz shifted the physical cutoff to 2.5 × 20/50 = 1.0 
Hz. Correcting the bridge time unit alone would not change those coefficients. 
Independent reconstruction 
Corner-load formulas reproduced logged raw CoP with a maximum per-round RMSE of 2.03 × 10⁻⁸. The 
recorded selected outputs were independently replayed using the stated recurrences. The first five seconds 
were excluded when comparing outputs because filter state already existed before round logging began. 
Table 2. Largest per-round reconstruction RMSE across both axes 
Condition Maximum RMSE Interpretation 
Median 0 Same median values after startup 
Moving average 7.83 × 10⁻⁷ Agreement within floating-point accumulation effects 
Butterworth 9.77 × 10⁻⁸ Supports the stated realised coefficients 
Alpha beta 5.13 × 10⁻⁷ Constant 0.05 s replay closely matches logged position 
 
These are numerical consistency checks, not independent board accuracy or device latency measurements. For constant 
intervals, rescaling velocity by Δt explains why alpha beta position output can remain unchanged; this does not validate 
corrupted source timestamps.

7 
Evaluation metrics for performance and smoothness 
A game-recorded value is stored directly by Unity, such as a hit event. A derived metric is calculated afterward 
from those logs, such as hit rate or jitter ratio. Unless stated otherwise, signal metrics used valid samples after 
the first five seconds, separately for x and y and each round. Axis results were averaged within each round, 
then the four round results were averaged per participant. 
Resolved target hit rate 
Definition and formula. Hit rate was the percentage of resolved balloons that were successfully burst. H is the 
number of hit events and L the number of miss events. 
Hit rate (%) = 100 × HH + L 
Calculation and units. Events were counted by type and checked against the final score and miss counters. 
Overall rates used total hits divided by total resolved targets, not the unweighted average of round 
percentages. Units were percent; hits and misses were counts. 
Significance. A higher rate means better observed success on resolved targets. It is a task outcome, not a pure 
filter score. It depends on skill, calibration, target presentation and filter behaviour. Balloons still in flight at 
completion were counted separately and excluded. Their exclusion favours neither a claim of complete 
exposure nor a causal filter comparison. 
Jitter ratio 
Definition. Jitter ratio compared the spread of consecutive changes in filtered CoP with the spread of 
consecutive changes in raw CoP. Let x[n] be raw CoP and y[n] the selected filtered output for one axis. 
Δx[n] = x[n] − x[n−1];     Δy[n] = y[n] − y[n−1] 
J = s(Δy)s(Δx)     Jround = (JML + JAP)/2 
Here s is sample standard deviation with denominator K − 1 for K differences. Differences were computed 
between adjacent valid retained samples. There were no within-round sequence gaps in the supplied Unity 
logs. The ratio has no units because numerator and denominator use the same CoP units. 
Interpretation. J < 1 indicates less rapid sample-to-sample variation; J = 1 indicates similar variation; J > 1 
indicates more variation. For example, J = 0.75 means the standard deviation of successive changes is 25% 
lower, not that 25% of sensor noise was removed. Genuine corrective movement can also be reduced. 
Significance and limits. This is a compact smoothness measure for comparing outputs produced from the same 
input. It cannot establish accuracy, responsiveness or noise suppression on its own. Strong smoothing may look 
good by this measure while delaying useful movement. A nearly constant raw signal would also make the ratio 
unstable; that was not the case in the analysed gameplay segments. 
Control standard deviation, samples at the control limit, regional target hit rates and path-length ratio were intentionally 
excluded from the main evaluation. They were not necessary to explain the selected filter comparisons.

8 
Evaluation metric for estimated signal lag 
Definition and formula 
Estimated signal lag described the time shift that best aligned a filtered CoP trace with its raw trace. It was 
calculated offline, not measured by the game as a dedicated latency test. For each axis and round, both 
retained signals were mean-subtracted and correlated over overlapping samples. 
C[k] = Σ (x[n] − x̄)(y[n+k] − ȳ) 
The sum covers only indices present in both signals. Correlation was divided by the square root of the product 
of their full-segment energies; this constant normalization does not change the maximizing lag. The search 
covered −10 to +10 samples, or nominally ±0.5 s. Positive k meant the filtered output followed the raw input. 
k₀ = arg max C[k];     laginteger = 1000 k₀ / fₛ milliseconds 
Why the report contains values below 50 ms 
A direct peak can occur only at integer offsets such as 0, 50, 100 or 250 ms at 20 Hz. A three-point parabola 
around that peak estimated the location between samples. With C₋, C₀ and C₊ denoting correlation at k₀ − 1, k₀ 
and k₀ + 1, the interpolation was: 
δ = C₋ − C₊2(C₋ − 2C₀ + C₊)     lagestimated = 1000(k₀ + δ)/fₛ 
The small correction was bounded to ±0.5 sample and applied only to an interior peak with a nonzero 
curvature. Estimates were then averaged across axes and rounds. This procedure reproduced the earlier 
approximately 47, 98, 233 and 7 ms values. The fractional values are model-based estimates; they do not 
demonstrate millisecond timing precision from a 20 Hz stream. 
Significance and limitations 
Smaller positive lag means less temporal trailing for that recorded movement. The estimate depends on the 
movement spectrum, finite record length and the correlation peak shape. A heavily smoothed output is not an 
exact shifted copy of the input, so one number summarizes rather than completely characterizes its timing. 
Signal lag excludes Bluetooth acquisition delay, Recorder buffering, file polling, UDP transport, rendering and 
display delay. It is not participant reaction time or complete board-to-screen latency. Those require an external 
synchronized response test. Theoretical group delay at one frequency is a useful consistency check, but is not 
expected to equal a broadband cross-correlation lag exactly. 
Integer peak results are retained alongside interpolated estimates in Table 5 so that the sample resolution remains visible. No 
claim of agreement to within a few milliseconds is made.

9 
Frequency response and raw signal spectrum 
Frequency response and cutoff 
Definition and formula. For an LTI filter, the transfer function gives the output-to-input complex amplitude ratio 
for a sinusoid. Evaluating z on the unit circle gives its discrete frequency response. 
H(z) = Σ bᵢz⁻ⁱ1 + Σ aⱼz⁻ʲ     z = exp(j2πf/fₛ);     gain = |H(z)| 
Significance. Gain near 1 preserves sinusoidal amplitude; gain below 1 attenuates it; gain above 1 amplifies it. 
The low-pass −3 dB point is the first frequency at which gain falls to 1/√2, about 0.707 of the DC amplitude. It is 
a gradual transition, not a boundary beyond which all movement disappears. Tables report gain at 1 and 5 Hz 
and the cutoff calculated at 20 Hz. 
The median is nonlinear, so it has no single input-independent LTI transfer function. Its response was instead 
evaluated with common step, ramp and isolated-spike inputs. For alpha beta, the LTI calculation assumes fixed 
gains and fixed Δt after initialization. 
Phase and group delay 
τg(ω) = − d arg H(exp(jω))dω  samples;     τg,ms = 1000 τg/fₛ 
Group delay describes how a narrow band of nearby frequencies is delayed by filter phase. It was evaluated at 
0.5 Hz from a centred numerical phase derivative. A larger value can contribute to temporal trailing of body 
movement, but it does not measure human reaction time. The moving average has a 100 ms group delay away 
from its response zeros; other filters vary with frequency [3]. 
Raw spectrum from Welch averaging 
Definition and calculation. An FFT separates a sampled signal into frequency components. Welch averaging 
estimates power spectral density (PSD) by averaging windowed segment spectra. Each round and axis used 
256-sample periodic Hann windows, 128-sample overlap, segment mean removal and a one-sided density at 
nominal 20 Hz. Frequency-bin spacing was 20/256 = 0.078125 Hz [2]. 
Power share below f₀ (%) = 100 ×

Integrals used trapezoids with interpolation at 0.5 or 1 Hz; shares were averaged equally across rounds. PSD 
units were CoP-ratio squared per Hz and shares were percentages. The spectrum identified where recorded 
movement power was concentrated. It did not separate intended lean, natural sway and sensor noise. The 
Nyquist frequency was 10 Hz; the recordings cannot establish absence of aliased higher-frequency components.

10 
Results and dataset integrity 
The analysis included all 16 completed sample logs and their 16 event logs, grouped by participant and seed. 
Counts were recalculated from the files rather than copied from the earlier report. Raw Recorder files and 
bridge audit files were used to check acquisition format and the timestamp-unit problem.

Event clock discrepancy 
Fifteen completion timestamps were within about 0.006 s of 90 s. Akshat’s seed 155921 round ended at 
91.040403 s on the event stopwatch. The game timer used Unity game time while the event logger used an 
unpaused stopwatch, so pausing or a timing interruption could create such a difference; the logs do not identify 
its cause. The recorded final score was retained. 
The event-time breakdown in Table 7 uses 0 to 30 s, 30 to 60 s and 60 s to completion. Its last interval is longer for that round, so 
it is not an exact reconstruction of all game-time difficulty phases.

12 
Common input comparison and theoretical validation 
Every filter was independently applied to every valid recorded raw x and y stream: 16 rounds × 2 axes = 32 
signals. Each replay began at the first valid logged sample, used the same causal recurrence as the game and 
was evaluated after five seconds. This is a computational comparison on identical inputs, not an additional 
participant experiment. 
Table 8. Same-input replay averages across 32 raw signals 
Filter Jitter ratio Estimated lag ms 
Median 0.983 48.3 
Moving average 0.796 97.7 
Butterworth 0.669 233.5 
Alpha beta 0.972 7.1 
 
Table 9. Linear-filter response calculated at nominal 20 Hz 
Filter Gain 1 Hz Gain 5 Hz First −3 dB Group delay 0.5 Hz 
Moving average 0.904 0.200 1.803 Hz 100.0 ms 
Butterworth as used 0.707 0.025 1.000 Hz 264.0 ms 
Alpha beta 1.000 0.840 No crossing below 10 Hz 10.2 ms 
 
Interpretation of the common input results 
The same-input replay gave a jitter ratio of 0.669 for Butterworth, 0.796 for moving average, 0.983 for median 
and 0.972 for alpha beta. These values compare filters on the same movements, whereas Table 4 also reflects 
differences in the four participants’ raw inputs. Both analyses consistently show the largest lag in the realised 
Butterworth condition. 
A filter order or sample window does not by itself determine performance. The Butterworth design is recursive, 
the moving average has finite sample memory, and the alpha beta predictor includes both position and velocity 
state. Their different gains and phases explain why equal-looking smoothing can produce different tracking 
behaviour.

13 
Frequency response validation 
 
Figure 2. Calculated amplitude and group delay for the implemented linear filters. The median has no ordinary LTI curve. Moving-
average group delay is plotted below its first zero at 4 Hz. 
What the curves establish 
The realised Butterworth response is already down to 0.707 amplitude at 1 Hz, while the moving average 
retains 0.904 and alpha beta about 1.000. At 5 Hz, Butterworth retains 0.025, moving average 0.200 and alpha 
beta 0.840. These are sinusoidal amplitude ratios, not percentages of sensor noise removed. 
The 0.5 Hz group delays of 264.0, 100.0 and 10.2 ms distinguish their phase behaviour. Measured cross-
correlation estimates need not equal those single-frequency values because recorded CoP contains many 
frequencies. The agreement in overall delay scale supports implementation consistency, without claiming that 
the difference between estimates is a measurement error.

14 
Recorded input replay examples 
Figure 3 uses one recorded ML input from Arham’s first round and processes that identical input through all 
four filters. The displayed 71 to 79 s segment has the largest ML standard deviation among eight-second 
windows beginning at integer seconds 5 to 75. This explicit selection illustrates dynamic movement; Table 8, 
not this example, summarizes all recordings. 
 
Figure 3. Grey is the same raw CoP in every panel; the coloured curve is a different causal replay output. Horizontal positio n is 
receive time relative to the first logged sample. CoP is a dimensionless balance ratio. 
The median follows the input with a short shift on monotonic portions. The moving average rounds short 
changes and trails them. The realised Butterworth filter changes more gradually and lags reversals. Alpha beta 
remains close to the measurement. Apparent visual smoothness alone is insufficient to decide which output 
preserves the desired movement most accurately.

15 
Common step ramp and spike tests 
These newly calculated tests used ideal inputs at exactly 20 Hz, not participant recordings. Filters were 
initialized at zero before a step at 1 s, a one-second ramp, or a unit spike lasting one sample. They explain 
causality and transient behaviour without confounding participant movements. 
 
Figure 4. Causal responses to identical ideal step, ramp and spike inputs. Lines connect discrete samples for readability; th ey do 
not imply a higher acquisition rate. 
Table 10. Simulated transient response measures 
Filter First ≥50% of step Peak step output Peak spike output 
Median 50 ms 1.000 0.000 
Moving average 100 ms 1.000 0.200 
Butterworth 250 ms 1.044 0.142 
Alpha beta 0 ms 1.009 0.850 
 
The first step threshold is measured relative to the first step sample. Alpha beta immediately outputs 0.85 and therefore cro sses 
0.5 with zero additional sample delay; this is not zero device latency. Butterworth peak overshoot was about 4.44%; alpha beta 
about 0.89%. The median completely removed this isolated ideal spike, not every possible artifact.

16 
Raw spectral results 
 
Figure 5. Welch raw CoP spectra at nominal 20 Hz. Each round spectrum is divided by its integrated power before averaging, 
giving every round equal weight. The logarithmic axis exposes small high-frequency components. 
Table 11. Mean raw-signal power shares after the first five seconds 
Axis Power below 0.5 Hz Power below 1 Hz 
ML horizontal 78.6% 95.3% 
AP vertical 76.9% 94.5% 
 
Interpretation 
Most recorded gameplay variation lay at low frequencies on both axes. This supports designing the control path 
to preserve relatively slow leaning. It does not prove that everything above 1 Hz is noise: corrective 
movements, natural sway and artifacts can overlap in frequency. Nor does it establish low sensor noise without 
a labelled stationary reference. 
The revised power percentages differ from the earlier 75% and 94% claims because this report uses an explicit, 
reproducible Welch configuration and interpolates the band boundary before integrating. The revised values 
are the calculations reported here; the earlier percentages were not retained without a reproducible method. 
Relation to smoothness 
Taking successive differences emphasizes fast changes. For an LTI filter, the output difference spectrum is 
weighted by both the filter gain squared and |1 − exp(−jω)|². Consequently, jitter is influenced by the full input 
spectrum, not just gain at 5 Hz. A moving average also has sidelobes, so it does not uniformly attenuate more 
strongly at every increasing frequency. The median must be assessed directly because it is nonlinear. 
No residual-noise-at-rest, false-movement-per-minute or signal-to-noise ratio was calculated. The continuous recordings may 
contain pauses, but they do not identify standardized quiet-standing ground-truth intervals.

17 
Analysis for each team member 
Akshat and the three sample median 
Akshat recorded 110 hits out of 161 resolved targets, or 68.3%. The live jitter ratio was 0.991 and the 
interpolated lag was 47.5 ms; the direct correlation peak was one sample in both axes of every round. These 
measurements are consistent with a short trailing median on largely continuous motion. They do not prove 
that the raw sensor contained few artifacts, because the size and type of any artifacts were not independently 
labelled. In the common spike test the median rejected the entire isolated spike. This demonstrates the 
mechanism, not a measured gameplay improvement over raw input. 
Alka and the five sample moving average 
Alka recorded 90 hits out of 160 resolved targets, or 56.3%. The live jitter ratio was 0.746, corresponding to 
approximately 25.4% less spread in consecutive changes. The 97.9 ms interpolated lag agreed in scale with the 
two-sample 100 ms theoretical delay. Its common-input jitter ratio was 0.796, showing why different 
participant inputs must not be used as a pure filter comparison. A smaller window would reduce memory and 
delay, but also reduce smoothing. There is no evidence here that changing the calibrated lean range alone 
would improve the score. 
Arham and the second order Butterworth 
Arham recorded 83 hits out of 159 resolved targets, or 52.2%. The live jitter ratio was 0.720 and the estimated 
lag was 233.2 ms. On common inputs this condition produced the lowest jitter ratio, 0.669, and the longest 
estimated lag, 233.5 ms. The reconstructed output and frequency response verify that the realised cutoff was 
about 1 Hz. The later event-time hit rate was lower, but the experiment cannot establish that lag caused that 
decline. The result describes the realised filter, not the intended 2.5 Hz design. 
Dharti and the alpha beta predictor 
Dharti recorded 117 hits out of 160 resolved targets, or 73.1%. The live jitter ratio was 0.973; the direct 
correlation peak was zero samples and parabolic interpolation gave approximately 7.3 ms. The corrected 
transfer function gives gain 1.000 at 1 Hz, 0.840 at 5 Hz and group delay 10.2 ms at 0.5 Hz, not the earlier 1.18 
gain and 23 ms delay. This filter followed the measurement closely with little smoothing. The ideal step test 
showed only about 0.89% overshoot. The highest observed hit rate cannot be attributed to the filter 
independently of Dharti’s skill and calibration. 
Why the same input comparison matters 
The common-input ranking was consistent with the intended smoothing mechanisms: Butterworth reduced 
rapid changes most, moving average next, while median and alpha beta changed them less. That is a defensible 
comparison of signal processing. A ranking of human performance would require each participant to use every 
filter under equivalent target presentations.

18 
Conclusion for each team member 
Akshat 
The three-sample median gave a short, approximately one-sample delay with little change in the gameplay 
jitter measure. It was effective against an isolated ideal spike in the separate computational test. Akshat 
achieved 68.3% resolved-target hit rate. The study supports its use as a lightweight spike-rejection candidate, 
but does not establish a gameplay advantage over raw input. 
Alka 
The five-sample moving average provided predictable smoothing and a delay of about 100 ms. Alka achieved 
56.3% hit rate. Its sample window clearly illustrates the memory versus responsiveness trade-off. A three-
sample alternative should be tested on the same inputs and with the same participant before any performance 
improvement is claimed. 
Arham 
The Butterworth trial demonstrated the strongest smoothing and largest signal lag among the tested 
conditions. Arham achieved 52.2% hit rate. Its effective cutoff was approximately 1 Hz because 50 Hz design 
coefficients were executed at about 20 Hz. This is a configuration mismatch, not evidence that all second-order 
Butterworth filters are unsuitable for interactive movement. 
Dharti 
The alpha beta condition preserved responsiveness with limited smoothing, and Dharti achieved 73.1% hit rate. 
The corrected theoretical response and the small simulated overshoot are consistent with a high measurement 
weight. These results motivate a controlled follow-up but do not identify alpha beta as universally superior. 
Team conclusion 
The project successfully linked physical load measurements to a Unity game through an external Python UDP 
bridge while preserving raw and derived records. Four members contributed four labelled gameplay datasets 
with six nominal minutes each. Independent same-input replay and transient tests demonstrate how filter 
memory, order and frequency response affect smoothness and lag. The findings also expose the importance of 
correct timestamp units and sample-rate-aware filter design. 
The central experimental conclusion is a trade-off, not a winning filter: stronger smoothing can delay 
meaningful movement. The observed ranking of hit rates follows the opposite ranking of lag, but it remains an 
association because participant, filter and partly target presentation were confounded. Correcting those 
limitations would allow a stronger controlled performance comparison.

19 
Study limitations and next experiment 
Limits on the present conclusions 
• Only four participants were tested, each with one filter. Four repeated rounds are not four independent 
participants, and no significance test can remove this confounding. 
• Shared seeds did not preserve identical complete target sequences because target selection depended on 
active balloons. Later target exposure therefore differed between participants. 
• Timing was irregular around 20 Hz, source timestamps were scaled incorrectly, and the Butterworth design 
rate did not match acquisition. Frequency tables use the nominal sample-index model rather than an 
exactly uniform physical-time record. 
• Participant calibration used single samples and its values were not embedded in the provided CSV headers. 
Quiet-standing noise, end-to-end latency and subjective comfort were not measured in standardized 
labelled trials. 
• One event clock exceeded 90 seconds by about one second. Event-time bins cannot perfectly recover the 
corresponding game-time phases, and final in-flight targets were not scored. 
• No VR headset was used. These results concern desktop gameplay and do not establish VR comfort, safety 
or headset performance. 
Recommended follow up 
First correct the Recorder time-unit configuration to seconds and measure the current acquisition rate. Either 
design fixed filter coefficients for that measured rate or explicitly resample to a uniform timeline before 
filtering. For a 2.5 Hz second-order Butterworth design at 20 Hz, b is approximately [0.09763107, 0.19526215, 
0.09763107] and a is [1, −0.94280904, 0.33333333]. This is a proposed condition, not the condition used for the 
reported results. 
Next precompute target lists and have every participant play every filter in a counterbalanced order, with raw 
input included as a gameplay baseline if feasible. Keep filter, mapping and target settings fixed within each trial. 
Add labelled quiet stance and repeated comfortable lean transitions so that rest variation and response delay 
can be studied under known instructions. Use a consistent procedure for all members. 
Finally save a metadata record with participant code, calibration values, filter parameters, measured rate, 
sequence identifier, software revision and clock units. Keep game-time and monotonic event time separately, 
and record pauses explicitly. These changes would improve reproducibility; they have not been applied to the 
game or to the original recordings as part of this report revision.
